figures.alt: Illustration of two teenagers on a sled speeding down a snowy hill, with motion lines.
figures.caption: A fast sled has more motion energy than a slow one.

figures.alt: Photo of a wooden ramp propped on a stack of books with a marble at the top, a paper cup lying on its side at the bottom as a target and a strip of tape with tick marks on the floor.
figures.caption: What the Ramp test can look like: change only the ramp height and measure how far the target moves.

figures.alt: Top: a warm cup and a spoon, with a heat arrow along the spoon from the warm cup toward the cooler end. Bottom: two rows with a warm body on the left and cold air on the right. With no coat the heat arrow is thick and heat leaves fast. With a coat in between, the heat arrow is thin, so heat leaves slowly. A coat does not make heat; it slows the heat leaving.
figures.caption: Heat always moves from warmer to cooler. A coat does not add cold or heat: it slows the heat leaving your body.

figures.alt: Interactive: pick a clay ball, a hard ball or a super ball and see bars for energy before and after a bounce. The total is always 100.
figures.caption: Pick a ball and see that its energy of motion becomes a little heat, sound and bending. The total stays the same.

figures.alt: Interactive: a slider sets the ramp height and a toy car rolls down to push a block, farther from a higher ramp.
figures.caption: Raise the ramp and see how far the same car pushes the block.

figures.alt: Grouped bar graph of target distance in cm. Low ramp: 2, 2, 3. High ramp: 7, 8, 8.
figures.caption: The target moved 2, 2 and 3 cm from the low ramp, and 7, 8 and 8 cm from the high ramp. Same marble, same target: only the ramp height changed.

figures.alt: Line graph of temperature in degrees C over three readings: 40, 37 and 35. The line slopes down.
figures.caption: A warm object cooled from 40 C to 37 C to 35 C over three readings, as heat moved to the cooler air around it.
